analysis.one_liner: Bars most lawsuits against small-aircraft makers for crashes involving planes older than 18 years.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it 91-8, the House passed it by voice vote, and President Clinton signed it into law on August 17, 1994.
analysis.plain_summary: This law sets a deadline for suing small-aircraft manufacturers. If a crash involves a plane or part more than 18 years old, the victims or their families generally cannot sue the manufacturer for the deaths, injuries, or property damage it caused, with a few narrow exceptions. Before this law, companies could be sued under state law no matter how old the aircraft was.
analysis.who_benefits: General aviation aircraft manufacturers gain a shield against lawsuits over older planes. Claims that once could be brought under state law — including for crashes of planes built decades earlier — are barred after 18 years, so manufacturers no longer carry liability costs (and the insurance and legal expenses that come with them) for their older fleets. The industry argued those costs had pushed several makers to the edge of bankruptcy.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small-aircraft manufacturers like Cessna and Piper

how_it_helps.text: Sets an 18-year limit on civil lawsuits against aircraft manufacturers for deaths, injuries, or property damage arising from a general aviation aircraft accident, with certain exceptions.
Before the law, under the version first introduced, the limit was proposed as 15 years; the final law set it at 18 years for general aviation aircraft and parts.

analysis.who_pays: People hurt in crashes of older small planes, and the families of those killed, lose the ability to hold the manufacturer accountable once the plane or part is more than 18 years old. The costs of accidents caused by old defects shift from the companies that built the aircraft to the victims, their families, and their insurers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Crash victims and families of the killed

drawbacks.text: Once a general aviation aircraft or part is 18 years old, victims and surviving families generally lose the right to sue the manufacturer for deaths or injuries the aircraft's defects caused, so they bear those losses themselves.

Supporters of the limit argued at the time that liability lawsuits over planes two or three decades old were driving U.S. small-aircraft makers toward shutdown and costing jobs; opponents argued the limit forecloses legitimate claims from crash victims regardless of how strong the evidence of a defect is. Both cannot be fully true at once, and the law resolves the tradeoff in the manufacturers' favor.
The limit applies through federal law even where state law would otherwise allow the suit, preempting the remedies states had provided for their own residents.
Exceptions to the 18-year limit exist but are narrow, so most claims over older aircraft are barred.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the manufacturers and their workers, the law removes an open-ended liability burden that the industry said was existential. For the public, the cost is concrete but concentrated: crash victims of planes older than 18 years lose legal recourse that other consumers of defective products keep. It is a genuine tradeoff, deliberately resolved for the industry, and it applies nationwide regardless of state law.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the Senate 91-8, cleared the House by voice vote under a fast-track procedure, both chambers agreed to each other's small changes, and President Clinton signed it on August 17, 1994.

narrative.text: The Senate Commerce Committee reported the bill favorably in November 1993 and it was placed on the Senate calendar.
The Senate passed the bill on March 16, 1994, by a vote of 91-8, with 48 of 56 Democrats and 43 of 44 Republicans voting yes.
The House passed it on June 27, 1994, under a suspension-of-the-rules procedure, which allows a bill to pass quickly with limited debate and no roll-call vote.
The House amended the bill, and the final version set the limit at 18 years; the Senate concurred in the House amendment with an amendment on August 2, 1994, and the House agreed two days later.
President Clinton signed it on August 17, 1994, making it Public Law 103-298.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: General aviation aircraft manufacturers are better off: they won an 18-year shield against liability lawsuits over older aircraft, signed into law with near-unanimous congressional support. Crash victims and their families are worse off, having lost the right to sue over older aircraft.

sides.party_line_note: The Senate passed it 91-8 with 48 of 56 Democrats and 43 of 44 Republicans in favor; the House passed it by voice vote, and a Democratic president signed it.

industries.note: The law gives makers of small planes an 18-year limit on lawsuits for deaths, injuries, and property damage from older aircraft, with narrow exceptions. The industry's gain is the public's cost: claims victims could once bring under state law are now barred, so accident costs shift to victims and their insurers.
The 18-year limit eliminates a large category of lawsuits against aircraft makers. Their interest here runs alongside crash victims', since the claims barred by the law are the victims' own.

industries.industry: Aircraft insurers and owners of older small planes
industries.note: With manufacturer liability capped by time, owners of aging aircraft face a market that industry said had been drying up over liability fears, and insurers face less exposure on older fleets. These gains are secondary to the core liability shift to crash victims.
